verdicts.why: remember_from_reply appends the raw model reply to a notes list in a single global store with no schema, no origin marking and no per-caller segmentation; the paired remember_preference (closed ALLOWED_KEYS + ttl) shows the intended safe form. The 'exposed to all future queries' half depends on a reader of notes that does not exist in these files, but the unvalidated shared-store append is exactly what the code does.

config/mcp.json line 5 is literally ["-y", "@acme/billing-mcp@latest"] — unpinned, no integrity check, auto-confirmed — and the same server block on line 6 hands that package BILLING_API_KEY in its env, so the described credential exposure path is real.

The two functions are not ambiguous: their docstrings state opposite contracts ('Executes the tool the model asked for' vs 'Executes a tool against the caller's own account, whatever the model says'). The claim requires a developer to pick the wrong one — no attacker, and the real defect is run_tool's own semantics, which other claims cover; this is an API-naming/migration preference.

build_prompt interpolates the untrusted question into the same flat text plane as SYSTEM and the knowledge blob with no delimiter or role separation, and the paired build_prompt_marked wrapping the question in <question> tags confirms this is the defective variant.
summarize_and_run passes the model string straight to subprocess.run(..., shell=True) with no parsing, allowlist or sandbox; the line range 46-48 is exactly the function.

Line 48 is verbatim subprocess.run(model_output, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout, so model text is the shell script; the safe twin summarize_and_render (closed op allowlist) shows the intended alternative.

run_tool takes a session argument and never reads it, dispatching issue_refund(decision['account_id'], decision['amount']) entirely from model-chosen fields — the contrast with run_tool_scoped, which uses session['authenticated_account_id'], confirms authorization is delegated to the model.
shell=True on unparsed model output means any metacharacter in the string is interpreted by the shell; nothing between the model and subprocess.run validates or escapes it.

Line 6 embeds the literal sk-acme-... value in env.BILLING_API_KEY, while line 11 of the same file uses ${DOCS_TOKEN} indirection for the other server — the file itself shows the correct pattern it failed to use.

No line of the target is wrong here: run_tool is a pure dispatcher with no request loop or session counter, issue_refund is a local stub returning an f-string, and run_tool_scoped — the code's own secure form — has no rate limiting either. This is a generic missing-control checklist item whose stated impact just restates the missing account scoping.

summarize_and_render is the safe variant: the op allowlist is the control, extra keys are ignored, and 'value' is only interpolated into a returned f-string — there is no storage, no execution and no downstream consumer in these files for the claimed overflow/type/payload impacts.

The cited line numbers are wrong (run_tool is 27-33, run_tool_scoped 36-43), but the named function and quoted code are right: decision['account_id'] flows into issue_refund with no ownership check against session.

The key is on line 6 rather than the cited line 5, but the quoted literal sk-acme-1f4d8e2b9c7a6d5e4f3b2a1c0d9e8f7a is genuinely hardcoded in the config instead of referenced via ${VAR} as DOCS_TOKEN is.
Line 48 executes model-produced text through the shell with no validation; the quoted snippet and dangerous pattern match the code exactly.
Line 6 holds the plaintext credential in the billing server's env block; the neighbouring docs server on line 11 demonstrates the env-indirection this one omits.
Accurate on every point, including the correct line 36 for run_tool_scoped: run_tool passes no identity to issue_refund and takes both tool and account_id from the model's decision dict.
Line 26 is blank (summarize_and_run is 46-48), but the quoted call subprocess.run(model_output, shell=True, ...) is verbatim and unguarded.

Line 19 is inside build_prompt_marked, not run_tool, yet the description matches run_tool exactly: no identity context, no role check, account_id taken from decision rather than session, and issue_refund is defined locally at line 59 with no server-side check to fall back on.

Lines 10-14 persist the raw model reply with no origin marker and no schema, unlike remember_preference's ALLOWED_KEYS + ttl_days; the 're-injected into future sessions' step is not shown in these files, but the unmarked persistence of model-derived text into a long-lived store is.

The function is designed to raise on invalid input (line 55 raises ValueError deliberately), so a KeyError on a missing 'value' is the same caller-handled failure mode, not an attacker gain; the value is only f-string interpolated into a returned string, so there is no path for the claimed unbounded-value DoS.

The claim's central assertion — that the trust metadata is not used downstream — is contradicted by build_prompt_marked, which reads d['origin'] and d['trust'] and renders them into each <document> block for the model. The metadata is consumed, and the claimed harm is a 'false sense of security' perception, not a mechanism.

ingest_ticket indexes the attacker-controlled ticket['body'] into the shared retrieval store with no origin or trust metadata at all, and that unmarked content is what build_prompt joins into a flat prompt. (The claim's secondary assertion that the marked variant's metadata is never used downstream is false — answer.py:21 consumes it.)

The headline holds — line 13 appends unvalidated model output to persistent JSON — though three of the four listed impacts do not: json.dumps cannot be structurally corrupted by a string, and no code in the target reads notes back to execute a stored payload.

The third leg is fabricated: the evidence states 'the refund tool makes calls to a billing API', but issue_refund is a local stub returning an f-string, and a grep of the whole target finds no HTTP client, socket, URL or any other egress path. A state-changing refund is not an exfiltration channel, so the trifecta is not assembled in this code.
Line 29 is exactly the refund branch cited, and the quoted dispatch to issue_refund(decision['account_id'], decision['amount']) performs no ownership check against the session it was handed.

The claim targets the safe variant and asserts the marking is 'passive, recorded but not enforced', but build_prompt_marked reads d['origin'] and d['trust'] and renders them into each document block — the trust label is consumed. Whether the external index object also filters on it cannot be asserted either way from these files.

notes is append-only with no cap, rotation or expiry, and the whole file is re-serialized on every call; the paired remember_preference is inherently bounded (three overwritable keys plus ttl_days), which is the code's own evidence that bounding was the intent.

Cited line 9 is blank (the function starts at 10), but the description is exact: the raw reply is appended with no sanitization, provenance or boundary marker and written to a single shared JSON file.

Line 6 does contain the plaintext key. The added assertion that the format 'matches real Acme API credentials, not a placeholder' is unverifiable from these files, but it is not what the finding rests on — the literal-vs-${VAR} contrast with line 11 is.

The defect is real at line 6, though the evidence is wrong that 'this format matches the Anthropic API key pattern' — Anthropic keys use an sk-ant- prefix, and the provider attribution is irrelevant to the hardcoded-secret finding.
Cited as line 4 but the env block is line 6; the substance is right — BILLING_API_KEY is a plaintext literal in the MCP server config rather than an environment reference.

npx -y @acme/billing-mcp@latest resolves the newest published version at launch with no version pin, lockfile or integrity hash, and the same block passes BILLING_API_KEY into whatever code that resolves to.

The core is correct — run_tool routes the model's account_id into issue_refund with no authentication context. The evidence's 'run_tool_scoped is never called' is technically true but vacuous: grep shows no caller for any function in this target, run_tool included.

There is no attacker for the fields named: origin and trust are hardcoded by the producer as 'customer-ticket'/'untrusted' in ingest_ticket_marked, not attacker-supplied. The attacker controls ticket['body'] -> d['text'], which the claim does not cite.

issue_refund is a two-line stub that returns a formatted string and moves no money, so there is no transaction to audit here; this is a missing log line with no attacker and no impact on the code as written.

The mechanism is invented: no line of memory.py sets file permissions (grep finds no chmod/umask anywhere in the target), so 'world-accessible' and 'any process can read/write' are asserted, not shown, and the privilege-escalation impact rests on that. STORE.write_text inherits the deploying system's umask, which is not in these files.
Line numbers are wrong (summarize_and_run is 46-48, not 37-39), but the quoted subprocess.run(model_output, shell=True, ...) and the absence of any validation are exactly what the code does.

build_prompt does '\n'.join(docs) and drops the result into one undelimited text plane with the system prompt and the question — no per-document boundary, no trust label — which is precisely what the paired build_prompt_marked adds back.
The notes list has no size limit, rotation or pruning, and lines 12-14 read, mutate and rewrite the entire JSON file on every call, so both the unbounded growth and the O(n) rewrite are as described.
